questions.question: Which equation shows the hydrogen phosphate ion, $\mathrm{HPO_4^{2-}}$, acting as a Brønsted–Lowry acid?
questions.answer: An acid donates a proton. In C, $\mathrm{HPO_4^{2-}}$ gives $\mathrm{H^+}$ to $\mathrm{NH_3}$, forming $\mathrm{PO_4^{3-}}$ and $\mathrm{NH_4^+}$. (A shows dissociation without a proton acceptor; in B and D it accepts a proton, acting as a base.)

questions.question:
Which is the correct equilibrium expression for the following reaction?
$$\mathrm{Fe_3O_4(s) + 4H_2(g) \rightleftharpoons 3Fe(s) + 4H_2O(g)}$$
questions.answer: Solids are left out of the expression, and each concentration is raised to the power of its coefficient: $K_{eq} = \dfrac{[\mathrm{H_2O}]^4}{[\mathrm{H_2}]^4}$.

questions.question: How many chain isomers are there that are carboxylic acids with the formula $\mathrm{C_4H_8O_2}$?
questions.answer: Butanoic acid and 2-methylpropanoic acid: 2.

questions.question:
Nitrogen dioxide decomposes according to the following equation.
$$\mathrm{2NO_2(g) \rightleftharpoons 2NO(g) + O_2(g)} \qquad \Delta H = +114 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$$
A 0.413 mol sample of $\mathrm{NO_2}$ was placed in a sealed flask of fixed volume and heated at a constant temperature until equilibrium was reached. At equilibrium the flask contained 0.170 mol of $\mathrm{O_2}$ gas. Calculate the amount, in mol, of $\mathrm{NO_2}$ and NO at equilibrium.
questions.answer: Forming 0.170 mol $\mathrm{O_2}$ forms $2 \times 0.170 = 0.340$ mol NO and uses 0.340 mol $\mathrm{NO_2}$, leaving $0.413 - 0.340 = 0.073$ mol $\mathrm{NO_2}$.
options: 0.073 mol of $\mathrm{NO_2}$ and 0.340 mol of NO
0.243 mol of $\mathrm{NO_2}$ and 0.340 mol of NO
0.243 mol of $\mathrm{NO_2}$ and 0.073 mol of NO
0.340 mol of $\mathrm{NO_2}$ and 0.073 mol of NO

questions.question: What is the correct IUPAC name for $\mathrm{CH_3CH_2CHClCHOHCH_3}$?
questions.answer: The chain has 5 carbons. Numbering from the end nearer the OH gives the OH on C2 and Cl on C3: 3-chloropentan-2-ol.

questions.question:
Which of the following statements correctly describes members of the same homologous series?

I. They undergo similar types of chemical reactions.
II. They contain the same functional group.
III. Consecutive members differ by a $-\mathrm{CH_2}-$ unit.
IV. They all have the same empirical formula.
questions.answer: I, II and III are true. IV is false: e.g. methanol $\mathrm{CH_4O}$ and ethanol $\mathrm{C_2H_6O}$ have different empirical formulae.

questions.question:
Four solutions were prepared at 25°C. Which solution contains the highest concentration of ions?

| | Solution (aq) | pH |
|---|---|---|
| A | HCl | 1.6 |
| B | HCl | 2.4 |
| C | NaOH | 12.5 |
| D | NaOH | 13.1 |
questions.answer: HCl at pH 1.6: $[\mathrm{H^+}] = 10^{-1.6} = 0.025$ mol L$^{-1}$. NaOH at pH 13.1: pOH $= 0.9$, so $[\mathrm{OH^-}] = 10^{-0.9} = 0.13$ mol L$^{-1}$ — the highest, so D has the most ions.

questions.question: Which of the following compounds has a molecular ion peak in its mass spectrum at $m/z = 60$?
What is the concentration (in mol L$^{-1}$) of a barium hydroxide solution with a pH of 12?
questions.answer: pOH $= 2$, so $[\mathrm{OH^-}] = 0.01$ mol L$^{-1}$. Each $\mathrm{Ba(OH)_2}$ gives two $\mathrm{OH^-}$, so $c = 0.005$ mol L$^{-1}$.

questions.question:
The structures of three hydrocarbons are shown below.

**X**: $\mathrm{H_3C{-}CH_3}$   **Y**: $\mathrm{H_2C{=}CH_2}$   **Z**: $\mathrm{HC{\equiv}CH}$

Which statement correctly describes the shape around the carbon atoms in these molecules?
questions.answer: Four single bonds → tetrahedral; one double bond (three electron domains) → trigonal planar; a triple bond (two domains) → linear.
options: The carbon atoms in X, Y and Z are all tetrahedral because carbon forms four bonds.
The carbon atoms in X are tetrahedral, those in Y are linear, and those in Z are trigonal planar.
The carbon atoms in X are tetrahedral, those in Y are trigonal planar, and those in Z are linear.
The carbon atoms in X are trigonal planar, those in Y are tetrahedral, and those in Z are linear.

questions.question: Which of the following compounds will **not** produce a peak in the 1680–1750 cm$^{-1}$ range using infrared spectroscopy?
questions.answer: This range is the C=O stretch. Propanoic acid, 2-methylpropanal and methyl propanoate all contain C=O; propan-2-ol does not.

questions.question: Which graph shows the change in pH when an excess of solid magnesium hydroxide is added to water?
questions.answer: Mg(OH)$_2$ dissolves slightly, releasing $\mathrm{OH^-}$, so the pH rises from 7. Once the solution is saturated, $\mathrm{Mg(OH)_2(s) \rightleftharpoons Mg^{2+}(aq) + 2OH^-(aq)}$ is at equilibrium and the pH levels off (graph C).

questions.question: Which of the following infrared spectra could be that of propan-1-ol?
questions.answer: Propan-1-ol has an O–H bond (strong, broad absorption at about 3230–3550 cm$^{-1}$) and no C=O (no peak near 1700 cm$^{-1}$): spectrum A. (B and C have a strong C=O peak; D has no O–H absorption.)

questions.question:
An equilibrium exists between A, B and C.
$$\mathrm{A(g) + B(g) \rightleftharpoons 2C(g)} \qquad K_{eq} = 64 \text{ at 298 K}$$
When 5.0 moles of A is combined with 5.0 moles of B and added to a sealed 2.0 L flask, what is the concentration of C after reaching equilibrium?
questions.answer:
Initially $[\mathrm{A}] = [\mathrm{B}] = 2.5$ mol L$^{-1}$. At equilibrium $[\mathrm{A}] = [\mathrm{B}] = 2.5 - x$, $[\mathrm{C}] = 2x$:
$$\frac{(2x)^2}{(2.5 - x)^2} = 64 \Rightarrow \frac{2x}{2.5 - x} = 8 \Rightarrow x = 2.0,$$
so $[\mathrm{C}] = 4.0$ mol L$^{-1}$.

questions.question: Which of the following salts has the lowest solubility in g L$^{-1}$? (Use the $K_{sp}$ values on the HSC data sheet.)
questions.answer:
All four are 1:1 salts, so solubility $s = \sqrt{K_{sp}}$, then multiply by molar mass:
- $\mathrm{CuCO_3}$: $\sqrt{1.4 \times 10^{-10}} = 1.2 \times 10^{-5}$ mol L$^{-1}$ × 123.6 = $1.5 \times 10^{-3}$ g L$^{-1}$
- $\mathrm{BaSO_4}$: $\sqrt{1.08 \times 10^{-10}} = 1.0 \times 10^{-5}$ mol L$^{-1}$ × 233.4 = $2.4 \times 10^{-3}$ g L$^{-1}$
- $\mathrm{CaCO_3}$ and $\mathrm{PbSO_4}$ are much more soluble ($K_{sp}$ about $10^{-9}$ and $10^{-8}$).

Barium sulfate has the lowest molar solubility, but copper(II) carbonate is lowest in g L$^{-1}$ because of its smaller molar mass.

questions.question: A hydroxycarboxylic acid with the formula $\mathrm{HOCH_2CH_2COOH}$ ($M = 90$ g mol$^{-1}$) undergoes condensation polymerisation to form a polyester in which the average polymer chain contains 1200 monomer units. What is the approximate molar mass of an average polymer chain, in g mol$^{-1}$?
questions.answer:
Joining 1200 monomers releases 1199 water molecules:
$$1200 \times 90 - 1199 \times 18 \approx 86\,400 \text{ g mol}^{-1}.$$

questions.question: The titration curve shown was produced when NaOH solution was added to an acid. How many acidic protons does this acid possess?
questions.answer: There are two equivalence points (at about 10 mL and 20 mL), so the acid is diprotic: 2.

questions.question: The graph shows how the pH changes when sodium hydroxide solution is added to 15.0 mL of a 0.0288 mol L$^{-1}$ solution of a diprotic acid. What is the concentration of the sodium hydroxide solution?
questions.answer:
$n(\text{acid}) = 0.0288 \times 0.0150 = 4.32 \times 10^{-4}$ mol. The first equivalence point (10.0 mL) removes the first proton, so $n(\mathrm{NaOH}) = 4.32 \times 10^{-4}$ mol in 10.0 mL:
$$c = \frac{4.32 \times 10^{-4}}{0.0100} = 0.0432 \text{ mol L}^{-1}.$$

questions.question: Which of the following compounds will react fastest with Lucas' reagent (a saturated solution of zinc chloride in concentrated hydrochloric acid)?
questions.answer: Lucas' reagent substitutes Cl for OH; tertiary alcohols react fastest. B is 2-methylpropan-2-ol, a tertiary alcohol. (A is primary, D secondary, and C is a ketone.)

questions.question:
The two equations and $K_{eq}$ values have been given for reactions involving NO(g).
$$\mathrm{N_2(g) + O_2(g) \rightleftharpoons 2NO(g)} \qquad K_{eq1} = 4.3 \times 10^{-31}$$
$$\mathrm{NO_2(g) \rightleftharpoons NO(g) + \tfrac{1}{2}O_2(g)} \qquad K_{eq2} = 7.4 \times 10^{-7}$$
What is the $K_{eq}$ value for the following reaction?
$$\mathrm{N_2(g) + 2O_2(g) \rightleftharpoons 2NO_2(g)}$$
questions.answer:
Add equation 1 to twice the reverse of equation 2:
$$K_{eq} = K_{eq1} \times \left(\frac{1}{K_{eq2}}\right)^2 = \frac{4.3 \times 10^{-31}}{(7.4 \times 10^{-7})^2} \approx 7.9 \times 10^{-19}.$$

questions.question: The malonate ion, $\mathrm{HOOCCH_2COO^-}$, is classified as amphiprotic. Show, by writing two chemical equations, how this ion is amphiprotic.
questions.answer:
Acting as a base: $\mathrm{HOOCCH_2COO^-(aq) + H_3O^+(aq) \rightarrow HOOCCH_2COOH(aq) + H_2O(l)}$

Acting as an acid: $\mathrm{HOOCCH_2COO^-(aq) + OH^-(aq) \rightarrow {}^-OOCCH_2COO^-(aq) + H_2O(l)}$

(Water is accepted as a reactant only in the equation where malonate acts as an acid.)

questions.question: Pent-2-ene can undergo polymerisation under suitable conditions. State the type of polymer produced from pent-2-ene.
questions.answer: An addition polymer.

questions.question: Pent-2-ene, $\mathrm{CH_3CH{=}CHCH_2CH_3}$, can undergo addition polymerisation. Draw a short section of the polymer produced, including two repeating units.
questions.answer:
The C=C opens and the two former double-bond carbons form the backbone, carrying a methyl and an ethyl side group:
$$-\mathrm{CH(CH_3)}-\mathrm{CH(CH_2CH_3)}-\mathrm{CH(CH_3)}-\mathrm{CH(CH_2CH_3)}-$$
i.e. a four-carbon section of backbone, with $-\mathrm{CH_3}$ on carbons 1 and 3 and $-\mathrm{CH_2CH_3}$ on carbons 2 and 4, and open bonds at each end.

questions.question: The boiling points of the first six compounds in the straight-chain carboxylic acid and primary amine series are shown in the plot. Explain the trends shown.
questions.answer:
**Trend 1:** boiling points increase as the number of C atoms increases in both series. Longer molecules have more electrons, so the dispersion forces between molecules are stronger and more energy is needed to overcome them.

**Trend 2:** carboxylic acids have higher boiling points than primary amines with the same number of carbon atoms. Both form hydrogen bonds, but O–H is more polar than N–H (O is more electronegative than N), so the hydrogen bonds between acid molecules are stronger (acids can also form dimers). More energy is needed to separate them.

**Trend 3:** the difference in boiling point between the two series becomes smaller as the chain gets longer. Dispersion forces grow with chain length while the hydrogen-bonding contribution of the functional group stays the same, so the functional group makes up a smaller share of the total intermolecular forces.

questions.question:
Methanol can be synthesised from carbon dioxide at high pressure, according to the equation:
$$\mathrm{CO_2(g) + 3H_2(g) \rightleftharpoons CH_3OH(g) + H_2O(g)} \qquad \Delta H = -49 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$$
Justify, using Le Châtelier's principle, why chemists in industry perform this reaction at high pressure.
questions.answer: Le Châtelier's principle: if a system at equilibrium is disturbed, the equilibrium shifts to partially counteract the disturbance. There are 4 mol of gas on the left and 2 mol on the right. Increasing the pressure shifts the equilibrium to the right, which reduces the number of gas particles and so partially reduces the pressure. This increases the yield of methanol.

questions.question:
Methanol can be synthesised from carbon dioxide at high pressure, according to the equation:
$$\mathrm{CO_2(g) + 3H_2(g) \rightleftharpoons CH_3OH(g) + H_2O(g)} \qquad \Delta H = -49 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$$
Explain, using collision theory, whether a high or low temperature should be used to produce a high yield of methanol.
questions.answer:
A low temperature should be used.

By collision theory, a reaction happens only when particles collide with enough energy (at least the activation energy) and the correct orientation. Lowering the temperature lowers the average kinetic energy of the particles, so fewer collisions have energy at or above $E_a$, and both the forward and reverse rates decrease.

The forward reaction is exothermic, so the reverse (endothermic) reaction has the higher activation energy. Lowering the temperature reduces the fraction of successful collisions more for the reaction with the higher $E_a$, so the reverse rate falls by more than the forward rate.

Temporarily rate(forward) > rate(reverse), so the equilibrium shifts to the right until the rates are equal again, giving a higher yield of methanol (though the reaction is slower to reach equilibrium).

questions.question: The percentage ionisation of a 0.102 mol L$^{-1}$ solution of hydrofluoric acid, HF, is 2.53%. Calculate $K_a$ for HF.
For hydrofluoric acid, $K_a = 6.70 \times 10^{-5}$. Calculate the resultant pH when 105 mL of 0.102 mol L$^{-1}$ HF is added to 80.2 mL of 0.104 mol L$^{-1}$ NaOH.
questions.answer:
$n(\mathrm{HF}) = 0.105 \times 0.102 = 0.01071$ mol; $n(\mathrm{NaOH}) = 0.0802 \times 0.104 = 0.008341$ mol.

NaOH reacts completely: $n(\mathrm{F^-}) = 0.008341$ mol and $n(\mathrm{HF})$ left $= 0.002369$ mol, in $V = 0.1852$ L:
$[\mathrm{HF}] = 0.01279$ mol L$^{-1}$, $[\mathrm{F^-}] = 0.04504$ mol L$^{-1}$.

This is a buffer. Assuming $x$ is small:
$$[\mathrm{H_3O^+}] = K_a\frac{[\mathrm{HF}]}{[\mathrm{F^-}]} = 6.70 \times 10^{-5} \times \frac{0.01279}{0.04504} = 1.90 \times 10^{-5} \text{ mol L}^{-1}$$
$$\mathrm{pH} = -\log_{10}(1.90 \times 10^{-5}) = 4.72.$$
(Equivalently, $\mathrm{pH} = \mathrm{p}K_a + \log\dfrac{[\mathrm{F^-}]}{[\mathrm{HF}]} = 4.174 + 0.547 = 4.72$.)

questions.question:
Iron can be extracted from iron ore, $\mathrm{Fe_3O_4}$, at very high temperatures:
$$\mathrm{Fe_3O_4(s) + 4C(s) \rightleftharpoons 3Fe(s) + 4CO(g)} \qquad \Delta H = +675.4 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}, \quad \Delta S = +702.9 \text{ J K}^{-1}\text{ mol}^{-1}$$
Write an expression for the equilibrium constant for this reaction.
questions.answer: $K_{eq} = [\mathrm{CO}]^4$ (the solids are not included).

questions.question:
Iron can be extracted from iron ore, $\mathrm{Fe_3O_4}$, at very high temperatures:
$$\mathrm{Fe_3O_4(s) + 4C(s) \rightleftharpoons 3Fe(s) + 4CO(g)} \qquad \Delta H = +675.4 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}, \quad \Delta S = +702.9 \text{ J K}^{-1}\text{ mol}^{-1}$$
Using $\Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S$, $\Delta G = +464.5$ kJ mol$^{-1}$ at 300 K and $\Delta G = -168.1$ kJ mol$^{-1}$ at 1200 K. Explain why this reaction is performed at very high temperatures, using the information provided.
questions.answer:
$\Delta H$ is positive (unfavourable) and $\Delta S$ is positive (favourable), so whether the reaction is spontaneous depends on temperature. At low temperature the $\Delta H$ term dominates: at 300 K, $\Delta G = +464.5$ kJ mol$^{-1}$, so the reaction is non-spontaneous.

At very high temperature the $-T\Delta S$ term outweighs $\Delta H$: at 1200 K, $\Delta G = -168.1$ kJ mol$^{-1}$, so the forward reaction is spontaneous. Because the reaction is endothermic, a high temperature also increases $K_{eq}$, shifting the equilibrium towards the products so that useful amounts of iron are produced.

questions.question:
Bioethanol can be produced by fermentation:
$$\mathrm{C_6H_{12}O_6(aq) \rightarrow 2C_2H_5OH(aq) + 2CO_2(g)}$$
A government is considering increasing the proportion of bioethanol in transport fuels to reduce dependence on fossil fuels. The table compares ethanol with octane, a fossil fuel.

| Property | Ethanol | Octane |
|---|---|---|
| Molar mass (g mol$^{-1}$) | 46.1 | 114.2 |
| Standard enthalpy of combustion $\Delta H_c^\circ$ (kJ mol$^{-1}$) | –1367 | –5471 |
| Energy released per litre of fuel (MJ L$^{-1}$) | 21.1 | 34.8 |
| Mass of $\mathrm{CO_2}$ produced per MJ of energy released (g MJ$^{-1}$) | 71 | 69 |
| Net mass of $\mathrm{CO_2}$ over the entire lifecycle of the fuel per MJ of energy released (g MJ$^{-1}$) | 32 | 94 |

Calculate how much energy (in kJ) is released per gram of each fuel.
questions.answer:
Ethanol: $\dfrac{1367 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}}{46.1 \text{ g mol}^{-1}} = 29.7$ kJ g$^{-1}$

Octane: $\dfrac{5471 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}}{114.2 \text{ g mol}^{-1}} = 47.9$ kJ g$^{-1}$

questions.question:
Bioethanol can be produced by fermentation:
$$\mathrm{C_6H_{12}O_6(aq) \rightarrow 2C_2H_5OH(aq) + 2CO_2(g)}$$
A government is considering increasing the proportion of bioethanol in transport fuels to reduce dependence on fossil fuels. The table compares ethanol with octane, a fossil fuel.

| Property | Ethanol | Octane |
|---|---|---|
| Molar mass (g mol$^{-1}$) | 46.1 | 114.2 |
| Standard enthalpy of combustion $\Delta H_c^\circ$ (kJ mol$^{-1}$) | –1367 | –5471 |
| Energy released per litre of fuel (MJ L$^{-1}$) | 21.1 | 34.8 |
| Mass of $\mathrm{CO_2}$ produced per MJ of energy released (g MJ$^{-1}$) | 71 | 69 |
| Net mass of $\mathrm{CO_2}$ over the entire lifecycle of the fuel per MJ of energy released (g MJ$^{-1}$) | 32 | 94 |

Ethanol releases 29.7 kJ g$^{-1}$ and octane 47.9 kJ g$^{-1}$. Assess the government's proposal to increase the proportion of bioethanol in transport fuels. You should refer to the data provided in your answer.
questions.answer:
**Advantages.** Net lifecycle $\mathrm{CO_2}$ emissions are much lower for ethanol: 32 g MJ$^{-1}$ compared with 94 g MJ$^{-1}$ for octane, a reduction of about 66%. The $\mathrm{CO_2}$ released when ethanol burns is largely reabsorbed by photosynthesis in the crops grown to make the next batch, so it is close to carbon-neutral; octane releases carbon locked away for millions of years. Bioethanol is also renewable, which supports reducing dependence on finite fossil fuels.

**Disadvantages.** Direct combustion emissions are similar, and slightly higher for ethanol (71 vs 69 g MJ$^{-1}$). Ethanol releases much less energy: 21.1 vs 34.8 MJ L$^{-1}$ and 29.7 vs 47.9 kJ g$^{-1}$. A greater volume and mass of fuel is needed to travel the same distance (larger tanks, more frequent refuelling). Growing the crops also uses land, water and fertiliser, and can compete with food production.

**Judgement.** On balance the proposal is supported. The much lower net lifecycle emissions and renewability outweigh the lower energy density, which can be managed through blended fuels or larger tanks.

questions.question:
A chemist proposes a two-step method to synthesise pentan-2-ol from pent-2-ene via an intermediate, $Q$:
$$\text{pent-2-ene} \rightarrow Q \rightarrow \text{pentan-2-ol}$$
Write a reaction scheme for the conversion of pent-2-ene into $Q$, identifying $Q$ and any reagent(s) used.
questions.answer:
Addition of hydrogen bromide:
$$\mathrm{CH_3CH{=}CHCH_2CH_3 + HBr \rightarrow CH_3CHBrCH_2CH_2CH_3}$$
$Q$ is 2-bromopentane. (3-Bromopentane also forms, because the alkene is unsymmetrical; $Q$ is then converted to pentan-2-ol by substitution with aqueous NaOH.)

questions.question: Pentan-2-ol has been prepared from pent-2-ene. State how the chemist could use a chemical test to confirm that the pentan-2-ol is pure and does not contain any unreacted pent-2-ene.
questions.answer: Add a few drops of bromine water to a sample of the product. Pent-2-ene's C=C double bond would react with bromine by addition, decolourising the orange-brown bromine water. Pentan-2-ol has no C=C, so if the colour remains orange-brown, no unreacted pent-2-ene is present.

questions.question: Pentan-2-ol has been prepared from pent-2-ene. Explain how the chemist could use mass spectrometry and infrared spectroscopy to confirm that the pentan-2-ol is pure and does not contain any unreacted pent-2-ene.
questions.answer:
**Mass spectrometry:** pentan-2-ol ($\mathrm{C_5H_{12}O}$, $M = 88$) gives a molecular ion peak at $m/z = 88$; pent-2-ene ($\mathrm{C_5H_{10}}$, $M = 70$) gives one at $m/z = 70$. A spectrum with $\mathrm{M^+}$ at 88 and no peak at 70 shows no pent-2-ene is present.

**Infrared:** pent-2-ene's C=C bond absorbs at about 1620–1680 cm$^{-1}$. If the product's spectrum shows no absorption in this region (only the expected broad O–H at 3230–3550 cm$^{-1}$ and C–H peaks), no alkene is present. (The O–H peak alone does not show purity, because it appears either way.)

questions.question:
A chemist is provided with a sample of an organic compound, $X$. The following observations are made:
- $X$ is made up of 62.0% carbon, 10.4% hydrogen and 27.6% oxygen by mass.
- Oxidation of $X$ produces $Y$, which reacts with solid sodium hydrogen carbonate to release carbon dioxide gas.
- $X$ can be synthesised by the oxidation of $Z$, using pyridinium chlorochromate (PCC).
- $Y$ can be heated under reflux with $Z$ in the presence of an acid catalyst to make a sweet-smelling compound, $W$.
- $W$ has the molecular formula $\mathrm{C_6H_{12}O_2}$.

Identify the homologous series to which $W$ belongs.
questions.answer: Esters (formed from a carboxylic acid and an alcohol under reflux with an acid catalyst).

questions.question:
A chemist is provided with a sample of an organic compound, $X$. The following observations are made:
- $X$ is made up of 62.0% carbon, 10.4% hydrogen and 27.6% oxygen by mass.
- Oxidation of $X$ produces $Y$, which reacts with solid sodium hydrogen carbonate to release carbon dioxide gas.
- $X$ can be synthesised by the oxidation of $Z$, using pyridinium chlorochromate (PCC).
- $Y$ can be heated under reflux with $Z$ in the presence of an acid catalyst to make a sweet-smelling compound, $W$.
- $W$ has the molecular formula $\mathrm{C_6H_{12}O_2}$.

Give the structure and name of $X$. Justify your answer using the information given.
questions.answer:
**Empirical formula:** C : H : O $= \dfrac{62.0}{12.01} : \dfrac{10.4}{1.008} : \dfrac{27.6}{16.00} = 5.16 : 10.3 : 1.725 = 3 : 6 : 1$, so $\mathrm{C_3H_6O}$.

$Y$ releases $\mathrm{CO_2}$ with $\mathrm{NaHCO_3}$, so $Y$ is a carboxylic acid. $X$ is oxidised to a carboxylic acid and is itself made by PCC oxidation of the alcohol $Z$, so $Z$ is a primary alcohol and $X$ is an aldehyde.

An aldehyde with formula $\mathrm{C_3H_6O}$ is propanal, $\mathrm{CH_3CH_2CHO}$. Check: $Y$ = propanoic acid and $Z$ = propan-1-ol give the ester $W$ = propyl propanoate, $\mathrm{C_6H_{12}O_2}$ ✓.

$X$: propanal, $\mathrm{CH_3{-}CH_2{-}CHO}$ (C=O at the end of a three-carbon chain).

questions.question:
A chemist is provided with a sample of an organic compound, $X$. The following observations are made:
- $X$ is made up of 62.0% carbon, 10.4% hydrogen and 27.6% oxygen by mass.
- Oxidation of $X$ produces $Y$, which reacts with solid sodium hydrogen carbonate to release carbon dioxide gas.
- $X$ can be synthesised by the oxidation of $Z$, using pyridinium chlorochromate (PCC).
- $Y$ can be heated under reflux with $Z$ in the presence of an acid catalyst to make a sweet-smelling compound, $W$.
- $W$ has the molecular formula $\mathrm{C_6H_{12}O_2}$.

$X$ is propanal. A student incorrectly proposes that $Z$ must be butan-2-ol. Assess the use of mass spectrometry, infrared spectroscopy and carbon-13 NMR spectroscopy to distinguish between $Z$ and butan-2-ol.
questions.answer:
$Z$ is propan-1-ol (the primary alcohol oxidised by PCC to propanal).

- **Mass spectrometry — useful.** The molecular ion peaks differ: $m/z = 60$ for propan-1-ol and $m/z = 74$ for butan-2-ol.
- **Infrared — not useful.** Both are alcohols with similar bonds, so both show the broad O–H absorption at 3230–3550 cm$^{-1}$ and C–O/C–H peaks; IR cannot readily distinguish them.
- **$^{13}$C NMR — useful.** Propan-1-ol has 3 carbon environments (3 peaks); butan-2-ol has 4 (4 peaks).

So MS and $^{13}$C NMR can distinguish $Z$ from butan-2-ol, but IR cannot.

questions.question:
A conductometric titration was undertaken to determine the identity and concentration of an unknown acid solution. The acid was either acetic, hydrochloric or sulfuric acid. The acid solution was added to 25.00 mL of standardised 1.01 mol L$^{-1}$ barium hydroxide solution. The graph shows how the conductivity changed as the acid was added.

Identify the acid and justify your response with respect to the information given.
questions.answer:
The acid is sulfuric acid.

Initially the conductivity is high because of mobile $\mathrm{Ba^{2+}}$ and $\mathrm{OH^-}$ ions. It falls steadily as $\mathrm{OH^-}$ is neutralised by $\mathrm{H^+}$ from a strong acid. At the equivalence point (22 mL) the conductivity is almost zero, so there are almost no mobile ions. The salt must therefore be insoluble: $\mathrm{BaSO_4(s)}$, which precipitates. After equivalence, excess strong acid adds mobile ions and the conductivity rises sharply.

- It is not HCl: $\mathrm{BaCl_2}$ is soluble, so $\mathrm{Ba^{2+}}$ and $\mathrm{Cl^-}$ ions would keep the conductivity well above zero.
- It is not acetic acid: barium acetate is soluble, so the conductivity would not approach zero. Also, excess weak acid is only slightly ionised, so the conductivity would level off instead of rising sharply.

questions.question: Barium hydroxide solution is titrated with sulfuric acid. Write a balanced chemical equation, including states, for the reaction that occurs.
questions.answer: $\mathrm{Ba(OH)_2(aq) + H_2SO_4(aq) \rightarrow BaSO_4(s) + 2H_2O(l)}$

questions.question:
A conductometric titration was undertaken to determine the identity and concentration of an unknown acid solution. The acid was either acetic, hydrochloric or sulfuric acid. The acid solution was added to 25.00 mL of standardised 1.01 mol L$^{-1}$ barium hydroxide solution. The graph shows how the conductivity changed as the acid was added.

The acid is sulfuric acid. Determine the concentration of the acid solution in mol L$^{-1}$.
questions.answer:
Equivalence point (minimum conductivity) at $V = 22$ mL.

$n(\mathrm{Ba(OH)_2}) = 1.01 \times 0.02500 = 0.02525$ mol, and by the 1:1 ratio $n(\mathrm{H_2SO_4}) = 0.02525$ mol.
$$c(\mathrm{H_2SO_4}) = \frac{0.02525}{0.022} = 1.15 \text{ mol L}^{-1}.$$

questions.question:
25.00 mL of 1.01 mol L$^{-1}$ barium hydroxide solution is exactly neutralised by 22 mL of sulfuric acid. The initial temperature of each solution was 20.00 °C, and the mixture reached a maximum temperature of 26.85 °C at the equivalence point.

Assuming the density of the acid is 1.54 g mL$^{-1}$, the density of the barium hydroxide solution is 2.21 g mL$^{-1}$, and the specific heat capacity is 4.18 J K$^{-1}$ g$^{-1}$, calculate the enthalpy of neutralisation for this reaction.
questions.answer:
$m = 1.54 \times 22 + 2.21 \times 25.00 = 33.88 + 55.25 = 89.13$ g

$q = mc\Delta T = 89.13 \times 4.18 \times 6.85 = 2552$ J $= 2.552$ kJ

$n(\mathrm{H_2O}) = 2 \times n(\mathrm{Ba(OH)_2}) = 2 \times 0.02525 = 0.0505$ mol
$$\Delta H = -\frac{q}{n} = -\frac{2.552}{0.0505} = -50.5 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1} \text{ (per mole of water formed)}.$$

questions.question: Calculate the maximum mass of silver sulfate that will dissolve in 2.00 L of 0.500 mol L$^{-1}$ sulfuric acid at 298 K. ($K_{sp}(\mathrm{Ag_2SO_4}) = 1.20 \times 10^{-5}$)
questions.answer:
$\mathrm{Ag_2SO_4(s) \rightleftharpoons 2Ag^+(aq) + SO_4^{2-}(aq)}$, with $K_{sp} = [\mathrm{Ag^+}]^2[\mathrm{SO_4^{2-}}]$.

If $x$ mol L$^{-1}$ dissolves: $[\mathrm{Ag^+}] = 2x$, $[\mathrm{SO_4^{2-}}] = 0.500 + x \approx 0.500$ (since $x$ is small).
$$(2x)^2(0.500) = 1.20 \times 10^{-5} \Rightarrow x^2 = 6.00 \times 10^{-6} \Rightarrow x = 2.45 \times 10^{-3} \text{ mol L}^{-1}.$$
$n(\mathrm{Ag_2SO_4}) = 2.45 \times 10^{-3} \times 2.00 = 4.90 \times 10^{-3}$ mol

$m = 4.90 \times 10^{-3} \times 311.9 = 1.53$ g

questions.question:
An equilibrium mixture was established by placing some hydrogen iodide vapour in a closed vessel at 300 K.
$$\mathrm{2HI(g) \rightleftharpoons H_2(g) + I_2(g)}$$
If an equilibrium sample contains 53.2% iodine gas by mass, calculate the value of $K_{eq}$ for this reaction at 300 K.
questions.answer:
Take 100 g of the equilibrium mixture.

$m(\mathrm{I_2}) = 53.2$ g, so $n(\mathrm{I_2}) = \dfrac{53.2}{253.8} = 0.2096$ mol. $\mathrm{H_2}$ and $\mathrm{I_2}$ form 1:1, so $n(\mathrm{H_2}) = 0.2096$ mol $= 0.423$ g.

$m(\mathrm{HI}) = 100 - 53.2 - 0.423 = 46.38$ g, so $n(\mathrm{HI}) = \dfrac{46.38}{127.9} = 0.3626$ mol.

The volume cancels (equal numbers of moles of gas on each side):
$$K_{eq} = \frac{[\mathrm{H_2}][\mathrm{I_2}]}{[\mathrm{HI}]^2} = \frac{0.2096^2}{0.3626^2} = 0.334.$$

questions.question:
The infrared spectrum shown and the following NMR data are for a compound of formula $\mathrm{C_5H_{11}NO}$.

**$^{13}$C NMR:** chemical shifts 23, 25, 42, 174 ppm.

**$^{1}$H NMR:**

| Chemical shift (ppm) | Integration | Multiplicity |
|---|---|---|
| 0.9 | 6 | doublet |
| 1.9 | 1 | multiplet |
| 2.1 | 2 | doublet |
| 6.2 | 2 | singlet |

**Typical $^1$H NMR chemical shifts:**

| Type of proton | δ/ppm |
|---|---|
| R–C**H**$_3$ | 0.9–1.0 |
| R–C**H**$_2$–R | 1.2–1.5 |
| R–C**H**R$_2$ | 1.5–2.0 |
| –CO–C**H**$_2$– (aldehydes, amides, ketones or esters) | 2.1–2.7 |
| R–C**H**$_2$–NH$_2$ or C**H**R–NH$_2$ | 2.4–3.0 |
| –C**H**$_2$–O– (alcohols, ethers or esters) | 3.3–4.8 |
| R–N**H**$_2$ or R–N**H**R | 1–5 |
| R–CON**H**$_2$ or R–CON**H**–R (amide) | 5–9 |
| R–C**H**O (aldehyde) | 9.4–10.0 |

Identify and draw the structure of this compound, justifying your choice with respect to the information provided.
questions.answer:
The compound is **3-methylbutanamide**, $\mathrm{(CH_3)_2CH{-}CH_2{-}CONH_2}$.

- **Formula:** it contains one N and one O, consistent with an amide.
- **IR:** the absorption at 3300–3500 cm$^{-1}$ (a double peak, typical of $-\mathrm{NH_2}$) shows N–H bonds, and the strong peak at 1680–1750 cm$^{-1}$ shows C=O. There is no broad O–H, so it is not an acid or alcohol.
- **$^{13}$C NMR:** 4 peaks, so 4 carbon environments for 5 carbons. Two carbons must be equivalent, which indicates branching (two identical $\mathrm{CH_3}$ groups). The peak at 174 ppm is the C=O carbon of the amide.
- **$^1$H NMR:** 4 proton environments.
  - 0.9 ppm, integration 6, doublet: two equivalent $\mathrm{CH_3}$ groups (R–CH$_3$ range) attached to a CH (n + 1 rule).
  - 1.9 ppm, integration 1, multiplet: a CH (R–CHR$_2$, 1.5–2.0) bonded to the two $\mathrm{CH_3}$ groups and a $\mathrm{CH_2}$.
  - 2.1 ppm, integration 2, doublet: a $\mathrm{CH_2}$ next to C=O (–CO–CH$_2$–, 2.1–2.7), split by the single CH neighbour.
  - 6.2 ppm, integration 2, singlet: the $-\mathrm{CONH_2}$ protons (amide, 5–9), confirming a primary amide.

Putting the pieces together: $\mathrm{(CH_3)_2CH{-}}$ joined to $\mathrm{{-}CH_2{-}CONH_2}$, i.e. 3-methylbutanamide.
